title: Toward a Model Fragrance-Free Policy: An Indoor Air Quality Source-Control Framework for Accessibility and Inclusion
content: Background: Indoor air quality (IAQ) is an important public health and accessibility consideration.  Fragranced consumer products and other indoor emission sources can contribute to chemical exposures and may create barriers to access and participation for individuals with Multiple Chemical Sensitivity and other affected conditions. Variation in fragrance-free policy design and implementation highlights the need for evidence-informed guidance. Methods: This policy synthesis study builds on a companion scoping review of 63 fragrance-free policy and guidance documents.  An evidence-to-recommendation synthesis integrated these policy findings with lived-experience evidence, empirical IAQ research, scientific and technical literature, authoritative guidance, accessibility and human-rights principles, and relevant expertise to inform the proposed framework. Results: Core elements identified across existing policies included definitions and scope, source control, communication and education, procurement, monitoring, enforcement, and institutional accountability. This synthesis informed an integrated, implementation-oriented fragrance-free policy and IAQ source-control framework. Conclusion: The proposed framework positions fragrance-free policy as an institutional accessibility and IAQ source-control intervention rather than solely as a request for individual behavioural change. By prioritizing source control and institutional responsibility, it is intended to reduce avoidable indoor chemical exposures and barriers to participation. Empirical evidence supports its source control foundation, while prospective evaluation of the complete framework is warranted.
